spans.assertion: the analysis compared dark-skinned players (skin tone ≥0.75, N=9,396) to light-skinned players (skin tone ≤0.25, N=83,655) across 93,051 player-referee dyads
the adjusted risk difference was found to be +0.204 percentage points (95% CI -0.054 to +0.486), two-sided p=0.124
the primary finding is that dark-skinned players have a 0.2 percentage point higher probability of a red card but the result is not statistically significant
the adjusted odds ratio was found to be 1.175 (95% CI 0.937-1.473, p=0.164)
the overall conclusion is that the hypothesis is not supported because both CIs include the null and p-values exceed 0.05
the risk difference estimand was defined as adjusted for confounders and averaged across the covariate distribution (marginal standardization)
found risk difference point estimate +0.204pp, 95% CI [-0.054,+0.486]pp, two-sided p=0.124
the risk difference was adjusted for number of games, position, league country, height, and weight
the risk difference estimate is not statistically significant, with the CI spanning from a negative to positive difference
the odds ratio estimand was defined comparing dark- to light-skinned players adjusted for the same confounders
found adjusted odds ratio 1.175, 95% CI [0.937,1.473], p=0.164
the odds ratio result is not statistically significant, CI includes 1.0 and p exceeds 0.05
the unit of analysis was set as the player-referee dyad
the analytic sample comprised 93,051 dyads (83,655 light-skin, 9,396 dark-skin), 1,129 players, 2,739 referees, and 1,148 red card events
the outcome variable anyRedCard was defined as a binary indicator of receiving at least one red card, collapsing counts
found unadjusted red card rates of 1.215% for light skin and 1.405% for dark skin, an unadjusted difference of +0.190pp
the exposure variable darkSkin was defined as a binary indicator derived from the average skin tone rating
two independent raters assessed player photos to produce skin tone ratings
found inter-rater correlation of 0.923 between the two raters
found exact rater agreement of 76.8%
light skin was defined as an average rating ≤0.25
dark skin was defined as an average rating ≥0.75
medium skin tone dyads (0.25-0.75, N=24,094) were excluded to maximize contrast
five covariates were selected for adjustment: log games, position (12 levels), league country (4 levels), height, and weight, with stated reference categories
the covariates were chosen based on stated rationale: games for exposure opportunity, position and league for differing foul/refereeing rates, height/weight for physical attributes
21,407 dyads were excluded for missing skin tone ratings (no player photo available)
24,094 dyads were excluded for having medium skin tone to compare extremes
7,476 dyads were excluded for missing covariate data, primarily missing position or weight
found the final analysis dataset retained 93,051 of 146,028 original dyads (63.7%)
rater1 and rater2 ratings were averaged into one skin tone score
the averaged skin tone score was dichotomized into ≤0.25 vs ≥0.75 groups
red card counts (0,1,2) were converted to a binary any/none indicator
games were natural-log transformed to reduce right skew and improve model fit
a multivariable logistic regression was fit with the stated formula including darkSkin, log games, position, league country, height, and weight
found the darkSkin coefficient β₁=0.161 (SE=0.115, p=0.164)
cluster-robust standard errors at the player level were used to account for non-independence of dyads sharing a player
adjusted risks were calculated via marginal standardization (g-computation), predicting counterfactual outcomes under darkSkin=1 vs 0 and averaging
the 95% CI and p-value for the risk difference were obtained via nonparametric bootstrap with 1,000 iterations, percentile method, and a specific two-sided p-value formula
no fixed effects or weights were used in the model
cluster-robust standard errors accounted for player-level clustering
each dyad was weighted equally and not weighted by the number of games in the dyad
found model fit statistics: pseudo R-squared 0.099, log-likelihood -5,571.4, convergence after 9 iterations
found regression coefficients/ORs for darkSkin, log_games, height, weight, and league country dummies with associated CIs and p-values
found that more games strongly predicts more red cards (p<0.001)
found center backs have the highest red card risk (OR=2.99) and goalkeepers are also elevated (OR=1.95)
found France and Spain have higher red card rates than England and Germany
found no significant effects of height or weight on red card risk
found negligible standardized mean difference imbalance between dark and light skin groups for games, height, and weight
found dark-skinned players are more concentrated in England and France and less in Germany and Spain than light-skinned players
found dark-skinned players are more likely to be center forwards and less likely to be goalkeepers or attacking midfielders than light-skinned players
concludes that substantial confounding by league and position justifies the multivariable adjustment
found the bootstrap distribution of the risk difference is approximately normal with mean 0.198pp, SD 0.137pp, range [-0.180,+0.655]pp, median 0.190pp
found no extreme outliers or bimodality in the bootstrap distribution, supporting the percentile CI's validity
found baseline red card risk of 1.213% for light skin, a 16.8% relative increase for dark skin, and a number needed to harm of 490 dyads if causal
concludes the absolute effect is small but represents a substantial relative increase, with questionable practical significance
a Wald test on the logistic regression coefficient was used as an alternative to the bootstrap for inference
found Wald test z-statistic of 1.393 and p-value of 0.164
the Wald test result corroborates the bootstrap p-value, both indicating non-significance, with the difference attributed to testing the coefficient vs. the risk difference directly
players without photos were excluded due to missing skin tone ratings, noted as a possible source of bias
dyads with missing position data (a key confounder) were excluded, noted as a possible source of selection bias

spans.assertion: the analysis did not account for referee-level characteristics beyond country, and implicit bias measures were not used in the primary analysis
the dataset includes implicit association test (IAT) scores by referee country
interactions between player skin tone and referee country bias were not modeled
found that with only 132 red card events among dark-skinned dyads, statistical power to detect small effects is limited
multiple analyses were conducted (risk difference, odds ratio, sensitivity checks) though primary and secondary estimands were pre-specified

spans.note: caveat that dyad-level aggregation may mask game-level heterogeneity when inferring referee behavior
caveats about generalizability: single season, four countries, male players, first divisions only
caveat that causality cannot be definitively established despite adjustment for measured confounders

spans.assertion: the dataset includes referee country-level implicit and explicit bias scores
these bias scores were not incorporated in the primary analysis to focus on the direct skin tone effect
the outcome analyzed was any red card as a binary variable
red card count (Poisson/negative binomial) and red cards-per-game rate models were not used, though they might yield different conclusions
found yellow card rates were similar across skin groups (0.41 light vs 0.36 dark), interpreted as evidence against a pervasive bias explanation
restates that the hypothesis status is not supported
concludes the hypothesis is not supported, though point estimates (RD +0.204pp, OR 1.175) trend positive, evidence deemed inconclusive
gives reasons for inconclusiveness: CIs include the null, p-values exceed 0.05, and wide CIs reflect limited power given the rare outcome and small effect
even at the CI upper bound the effect would be modest, and its practical significance is debatable given observational data and possible residual confounding
gives a skeptical assessment that the point estimate could reflect chance, unmeasured confounding, or play-style differences rather than referee bias

a more definitive answer would have required a larger sample, experimental/quasi-experimental design, direct measurement of referee behavior, and control for additional confounders, none of which were carried out here
recommends not concluding that referees exhibit skin tone bias, as the evidence is insufficient at conventional significance levels
a fixed random seed (42) was set for bootstrap resampling and specific software versions (Python 3.11, pandas 2.x, numpy 1.x, statsmodels 0.14.x, scipy 1.x) were used for reproducibility
